overview: The Calusa built a powerful maritime society in southwest Florida, with Mound Key as a political centre. Fishing, shellworking and engineered waterways supported large communities without a farming-based economy. The map’s 1492 to 1530 window catches only a short part of a much longer history, whose older traces survive in mounds and waterlogged deposits.

periods.title: Before the first recorded Spanish coastal encounters
periods.summary: Calusa communities already occupied an engineered coastal landscape; 1492 is a map boundary, not their foundation.

periods.title: Early encounters
periods.summary: Ponce de León explored the coast in 1513 and was mortally wounded during a colonising attempt in 1521. Calusa political history continued afterward.

items.text: At Mound Key, researchers investigated large enclosed watercourts beside the main canal. Organic materials dated their construction to about 1300 to 1400. The team interprets them as places to hold live fish, requiring knowledge of water movement and fish behaviour. Dinner could keep swimming until it was needed.

Waterlogged deposits preserved palm-fibre cordage, wood, seeds, fish scales and bones. The bones include schooling fish such as mullet, pinfish and herring. These small remains let archaeologists test the fishing interpretation against actual contents, rather than guessing the purpose from the enclosure’s shape alone.

On the high shell mound, traces of a large building reveal several construction phases beginning around 1000. Spanish accounts later described the ruler’s house as holding 2,000 people. Excavation supports an exceptionally large building; the capacity remains a historical description rather than a count of excavated residents.

sections.title: A fish bone can change the story

items.text: Mullet can gather in predictable schools and can be preserved by dry-smoking. Yet early archaeological samples did not make them look especially important. Karen Walker revisited stored bone collections to test whether a Spanish observer’s account of a major mullet fishery fitted the physical evidence.

The reanalysis found that fragile bones, sample sizes and identification shortcuts had hidden part of the picture. Later Mound Key samples showed a stronger mullet signal than Pineland samples. The result suggests a fishery that varied by place and period, rather than one unchanging menu across the whole region.

sections.title: Shells became tools for making more things

items.text: At Useppa Island and Buck Key, unfinished tools, shell fragments, pounders and grinding implements identify workshop activity. Researchers linked these deposits to increased production after about 800. The piles preserve stages of manufacture: a broken or unfinished object can explain a craft better than a perfect museum piece.

Shell axes and adzes helped workers shape wood. Dietler’s study compared 441 tools from 93 archaeological sites and found evidence of exchange with neighbouring communities. His proposal that leaders strengthened their power by encouraging these industries is an interpretation built from that production and distribution evidence.

sections.title: Wood, nets and a remarkable cat

items.text: The 1896 excavation at Key Marco recovered netting, cordage, wooden bowls and boxes from wet deposits. Waterlogged preservation saved materials that often rot away. The collection makes daily life unusually tangible: coastal households needed containers, strong fibre and repaired fishing equipment as well as impressive buildings.

The Key Marco collection includes net weights and net-mesh gauges, alongside bone pins and points. A gauge helped a maker keep openings consistent as a net took shape. Catching fish began with careful handwork on shore, long before anybody paddled out onto the water.

The small wooden Key Marco Cat combines human and feline features. Its catalogue records differing published dates within the broad span 700 to 1500, and uncertainty over whether its maker was Calusa or a predecessor. Its survival shows extraordinary carving skill without allowing us to name the artist or translate its meaning.

sections.title: People carried their histories across the sea

items.text: Eighteenth-century slave raids and violence drove people from South Florida. Archival research follows Calusa and other refugees to Cuba in 1711 and again in 1760. These were people seeking safety, not an archaeological culture simply fading out of existence; the surviving records follow only parts of their journeys.

sections.title: Why there is no invented Calusa sentence here

items.text: The Randell Research Center reports that the Calusa left no written records of their own. Spanish accounts preserve outside descriptions, while carvings and other objects carry visual meaning that cannot be read as translated sentences. No securely readable original Calusa writing sample is known from the evidence used for this card.

ending.text: The 1530 map cutoff is not the end of Calusa power. Later encounters and resistance continued, while eighteenth-century slave raids, disease and displacement broke apart the political society. Refugees reached Cuba in several movements, including 1760. This process has no single securely established fall year, and displacement should not be confused with every person dying.
